title: Ankara Stages Aegean Naval Exercise as Greece-Israel Ties Strain Relations; Fund Crackdown Spreads to Ponzi-Style Managers
subhead: Turkey is deploying naval forces across four seas for the Denizkurdu-I exercise as Fidan calls Greece's island militarization a security threat, while regulators freeze seven asset managers and order 130 funds liquidated in the widening Pusula-led market crisis.

sections.heading: Denizkurdu-I: Ankara Sends Warships to Four Seas as Athens Goes on Alert
sections.body:
Turkey is preparing its Denizkurdu-I surface operations exercise from 20-24 September across the Black Sea, Sea of Marmara, Aegean and Eastern Mediterranean, Turkish Defence Ministry spokesperson Rear Admiral Zeki Aktürk confirmed Thursday. The exercise culminates 24 September with a Distinguished Observer Day in the Eastern Mediterranean aboard the TCG Anadolu, Turkey's amphibious assault ship and drone carrier, according to Neos Kosmos. It follows Denizkurdu-II in June, which Ankara said involved 125 ships and 60 air assets.

The timing is loaded. On 17 September, Turkey's Defence Ministry publicly criticized Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis' visit to Kastellorizo, under 3 km off the Turkish coast, arguing the island's military garrison contradicts its demilitarized status under the 1947 Paris Peace Treaty. Greek armed forces have been placed on heightened alert, with Hellenic Navy vessels, submarines and surveillance assets expected to track the exercise.
sections.whyItMatters: A large scheduled naval drill is one thing; running it amid an open war of words over Aegean islands and maritime jurisdiction raises the risk of an accidental encounter. Greece monitoring the exercise with heightened readiness means any close patrol is now a crisis-management test, not a routine drill.

sections.heading: Fidan Warns Athens Over 'Threat' as Greece-Israel 'Achilles Shield' Reshapes the Balance
sections.body:
Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, speaking during a visit to Azerbaijan, said Ankara regards Greece's militarization of Aegean islands as a security threat, per Politico and eKathimerini. 'The militarization of the islands that have a demilitarized status constitutes a threat for us,' Fidan said, adding 'we don't want Greece to become a tool in the hands of those who wish to destabilize the region.' Athens rejected the remarks as escalation, with Mitsotakis insisting Greece 'will not accept instructions from anyone on how to strengthen its defense capabilities.'

The underlying driver is military, not just rhetorical. Greece signed a landmark $3.5 billion (~€3 billion) air-defense deal with Israel, named 'Achilles Shield', building a multi-layered antimissile system, per AP. A JNS analysis calls it a 'defensive wall' that shifts the regional balance against Erdoğan, who has warned of a bid to 'encircle' Turkey. Ankara also complained last month about drone activity on Rhodes and rejects Greece's UNCLOS-based right to extend territorial waters to 12 miles, which Turkey has long warned it would treat as a casus belli.
sections.whyItMatters: The Greece-Israel 'Achilles Shield' deal turns a bilateral Aegean dispute into a confrontation between Ankara and a wider anti-Turkey axis. Fidan's language — calling Greece a 'tool' — signals Turkey sees Athens as being pulled into an alliance framework aimed at it, which raises the stakes of every naval drill.

sections.heading: Fund Crisis Widens: Regulators Freeze Seven Managers, Liquidate 130 Funds
sections.body:
Turkey's market turmoil, set off by the collapse of Pusula, has escalated into a broad crackdown. The Capital Markets Board (SPK) suspended trading in funds managed by seven asset managers — Tera, Pusula, Hedef, Atlas, A1, Pardus and Bulls Portfoy — and ordered 130 funds liquidated, with a combined portfolio of 891 billion lira (~$21.4 billion) and about 353,000 investors, per the Financial Times and Business Standard. SPK has also referred 38 people to prosecutors over suspected market manipulation. The Financial Stability Committee, chaired by Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek, held an emergency meeting Thursday and called the problem 'temporary and manageable,' concentrated in a specific part of the fund market.

The central bank stepped in with liquidity: raising repo funding to 300 billion lira and raising banks' interbank borrowing limits tenfold, per Reuters and Anadolu Agency. The BIST 100 fell about 8% across Tuesday and Wednesday, then rose up to 2.5% early Thursday after the steps before giving back some gains. State-owned Emlak Katılım has begun talks to acquire two Pusula-linked savings-finance companies, and officials are now publicly targeting what regulators describe as 'Ponzi-style' fund structures, according to Business Standard and MSN.
sections.whyItMatters: This is now a systemic-confidence event, not a single-firm blowup: 130 funds liquidated and 353,000 investors affected tests Turkey's market credibility in the run-up to a contested election year. The CBRT's liquidity backstop and the state takeover of Pusula-linked lenders show Ankara is determined to ring-fence the damage, but the 'Ponzi-style' framing suggests more cases may surface.

sections.heading: Ocalan Given Formal 'Technical Coordinator' Role in Disarmament Panel
sections.body:
Jailed PKK leader Abdullah Öcalan has been assigned a formal role as technical coordinator to oversee the group's disarmament and dissolution, Presidential Chief Advisor Mehmet Uçum told reporters in Ankara on 17 September, according to Xinhua via NTV. Uçum said Öcalan will serve on a newly formed state subcommittee under the 'Terror-Free Türkiye' process, which builds on a reintegration law parliament passed on 10 August. 'Whoever established the organization and made them use weapons is the one who will dissolve it,' Uçum said, stressing the decision does not mean Öcalan will be released or granted privileges.

The move institutionalizes what was previously an informal role: the PKK declared its intention to disarm and disband in May 2025 after a call from Öcalan, and Turkey and regional actors have been managing the transition since amid friction over the pace of reforms. The panel gives the jailed leader a formal seat in the process while Ankara keeps him in custody.
sections.whyItMatters: Formalizing Öcalan's role converts a fragile, personality-driven ceasefire into an institutional mechanism with named responsibilities — a real step, but one that will be judged on whether it accelerates actual disarmament and on the political reforms Kurdish parties continue to demand.

sections.heading: Erdoğan's Syria Visit Moves Closer as Ankara Pushes Trade and Integration
sections.body:
President Erdoğan is expected to visit Syria in the near future, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said in Damascus, as Ankara and the new Damascus government deepen ties, per The New Arab and Daily Sabah. Fidan reaffirmed Turkey's commitment to Syria's unity and stability after his two-day visit, and Ankara has stressed that the integration of armed groups under central state structure is 'essential for Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity,' per Anadolu. The Economist notes the visit has Israel worried about Ankara's growing influence in Damascus.

The trip, initially planned for April, was postponed after the Iran war broke out in February. Ankara has signaled a broader economic push alongside the security dimension, including expanded trade ties, though concrete dates and figures beyond the reported $10 billion trade ambition remain in development.
sections.whyItMatters: An Erdoğan visit would cement Turkey as the dominant external patron of Syria's post-war order — economic access in exchange for security alignment. Israel's concern cited by the Economist underscores how Syria policy now intersects with the wider Turkey-Israel friction.

sections.heading: COP31 Host Under the Spotlight: Turkey Faces Its Own Energy Transition Gaps
sections.body:
As host of the UN climate summit later this year in Antalya, Turkey is under fresh scrutiny over its own renewable targets, with Bloomberg reporting on 18 September that Ankara's electrification ambitions will require significant domestic policy changes to be credible. Turkey is pushing a global goal for electricity to meet 35% of world energy demand by 2035, a flagship COP31 initiative being co-proposed with Australia, according to Reuters and Oilprice.

Domestically, Turkey plans to invest $108 billion in renewable infrastructure targeting 120 GW of installed wind and solar by 2035, and renewables generated over 72% of its electricity in May — yet coal remains its largest single source of generation, and the country is simultaneously expanding oil and gas exploration, per Oilprice and MSN. COP31 President-Designate Murat Kurum insisted Turkey holds the 'final decision' over the summit despite Australia's role in negotiations, per Climate Home News.
sections.whyItMatters: Hosting COP31 while still leaning on coal exposes Turkey to awkward credibility questions on the world stage. The gap between its ambitious 2035 electrification pitch and its own coal-reliant power mix will be a central pressure point as the summit approaches.

bottomLine: Today the dominant story is the sharpening Turkey-Greece confrontation: Ankara is running a four-sea naval exercise amid Fidan's warning over Aegean island militarization, and the backdrop is Greece's new 'Achilles Shield' air-defense deal with Israel — a combination that turns a long-frozen rivalry into an active, high-risk theater. Meanwhile, Turkey's market crisis matured into a systemic test, with seven fund managers frozen, 130 funds liquidated and 38 people referred to prosecutors, forcing the central bank to inject liquidity as a contested election year nears. On the peace and energy fronts, Öcalan gained a formal disarmament coordinating role and Turkey faces its own credibility gap as COP31 host. The through-line: Ankara is asserting itself hard on security and stability fronts — the Aegean, the markets, Syria, the PKK process — while carrying elevated risk on each.
sources: Neos Kosmos, Politico EU, eKathimerini, Irish Times, AP News, JNS, Bloomberg, Reuters, Financial Times via Business Standard, Anadolu Agency, Xinhua/NTV, The New Arab, Daily Sabah, The Economist, Oilprice, MSN, Climate Home News, Algemeiner
